entries.text: Lin selected the microphone, then carefully closed the clear cover over the tape deck. The thirteen-year-old label stayed where it was.
It was neither rejected nor allowed to finish today's farewell for them. She pulled a chair toward the microphone, and its red lamp came on.
I thought you'd choose the old call, so all I would have to do was press a button. Now that we're recording, all I have is “good morning.”
Even my own name feels borrowed. But if the final record has none of us as we are now, I think I'll regret it.
Start with good morning; don't sum up thirteen years or speak for people who never had time to say goodbye. Say only what you know now.
There are two people in this room. In the final minute, they are still willing to hear each other out.
All right; signal me when the window connects, and I won't read from a script. If I stumble, don't ask for another take.
We aren't leaving the prettiest version—we're leaving proof that we actually stood here. Lin folded her three-line note beneath the tape box.
Zhou checked the send lamp and raised a hand without giving his usual countdown. Lin leaned toward the microphone and heard her own heartbeat.
His headphones touched the desk, and red level bars woke with her breath. When his hand fell, she did not look for the note.
“This is Cape Hill Community Radio. Good morning. In our final minute, we can still hear one another.”
When the receive lamp steadied, Lin wrote the transmission time in the log and signed her own name under Recorder.
They climbed the narrow stairs. She hung the headphones on the rail and left the folded script behind as the first light cleared the antenna.
I wasn't shaking in there, was I? I felt nothing when I finished, but now my fingers are cold; the feeling arrived late.
I always waited for you to tell me the next step; for those few seconds, nobody could call my voice back. So that is what deciding feels like.
Your voice was steady, and you slowed down on the last sentence just enough to make it clear. Ten seconds to the master switch.
This time you cut the power and I'll watch the lamp. If you sent the final call, the final action should be yours too.
An antenna cable swayed in the wind, carrying its last tremor into the roof beneath their feet. The new call had no old tape hiss.
It had none of thirteen years' weight, only one uncorrected breath crossing the morning roof into a record whose time began today.
Did the archive send a receipt? I want to know the words “one another” really arrived and weren't left inside our monitor speaker.
Check the recorder field too. I need to know this isn't an automatic shutdown notice completed by the line, with nobody inside it.
Received: new station call, eight point one seconds complete and unedited, marked as Cape Hill Community Radio's final live record. Sender and recorder: Lin Cheng.
Duty confirmation: Zhou Yao; “one another” arrived intact. You aren't only the person who came to clear the last shift anymore.
Good; it didn't speak for the past, only left proof that we were here. When the archive opens for searches, I'll add a note.
I'll include the names we couldn't fit into the call, then interview the people below who remember this station. Today won't be its only new voice.
Zhou called “ten seconds,” and Lin held the master switch until the status lamp went dark. Wind passed through an antenna no longer transmitting.
The city had already received the eight-point-one seconds she left behind. She led the way downstairs, carrying a blank tape label dated today.
This Moment, Archived
